facts.claim: Claude Code’s sandboxing docs say a sandbox needs both walls: without the network wall a taken-over agent could send private files such as SSH keys out, and without the file wall it could plant a backdoor in system files to get network access.
In Anthropic’s October 2025 design, the file wall lets the agent read or change only specific folders.
In Anthropic’s design, the network wall lets the agent connect only to approved servers, so a taken-over agent cannot leak private data or download malware.

By default a sandboxed command can read most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials, so credentials you do not want commands to read must be protected explicitly.
By default sandboxed commands can write to the working directory and a per-user temp directory; protected paths stay write-denied so a command cannot grant itself permissions.
In Anthropic’s design, the sandbox reaches the internet only through a proxy server outside it, which limits the sites a program can connect to and asks a person about sites not yet approved.

In Claude Code on the web, sensitive credentials such as git credentials or signing keys are never inside the sandbox; a proxy verifies the operation and attaches the real authentication token before forwarding the request.
In Anthropic’s own internal use of Claude Code, reported in October 2025, sandboxing safely cut permission prompts by 84%.
Anthropic’s sandbox is built on tools inside the operating system, bubblewrap on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS, so the operating system enforces its limits.

Allowing broad domains such as github.com can create paths for data exfiltration, because the proxy makes its allow decision from the client-supplied hostname without inspecting the encrypted connection's contents.
Allowing a sandboxed command access to a system socket such as /var/run/docker.sock effectively grants access to the host system through it.
Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary; review its limitations before relying on it as a hard security control.
gVisor is an application kernel that implements a Linux-like interface and provides a strong layer of isolation between running applications and the host operating system.
Firecracker runs workloads in lightweight virtual machines called microVMs using the Linux Kernel Virtual Machine, and was built at AWS to power services like Lambda and Fargate.

A bug in Anthropic’s sandbox-runtime before version 0.0.16 left the network sandbox unenforced when a policy allowed no domains at all, so sandboxed code could make network requests outside the sandbox (CVE-2025-66479, published December 2025, patched in 0.0.16).
